lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Dashboard That Lags on Purpose
text: Welcome to React Performance Patterns. I'm glad you're here, because this is one of those topics where most people have heard the vocabulary, memo, useMemo, useCallback, but very few have actually watched it make a measurable difference. That's what we're going to do in this course. We are not going to sprinkle optimizations around and hope. We are going to take an app that is slow on purpose, measure exactly where the time goes, and fix it one change at a time, checking after every change that the number actually moved. If a fix doesn't move the number, we throw it away. Okay? That's the rule for the whole course: measure, change one thing, measure again.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Dashboard That Lags on Purpose
text: So what are we building? A trading dashboard. Imagine the screen a trader keeps open all day. There's a table of five thousand rows, one per ticker symbol, and every row shows a symbol, a last price, a percent change, and a volume. Prices tick live, so rows keep updating several times a second. On top there's a filter bar where you can search by symbol, filter by sector, and sort by any column. The reason I picked this is that it is genuinely hard on React. Lots of rows, lots of updates, lots of derived data. If your tricks survive this app, they'll survive most apps you'll ever write.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Dashboard That Lags on Purpose
text: Let me show you the starting point. I'll open the project, and here's the structure. In the src folder we have App.jsx, Dashboard.jsx, FilterBar.jsx, PriceTable.jsx, and PriceRow.jsx. There's also a file called useTicks.js, which is a custom hook that fakes a live price feed with a timer. It updates a few hundred random symbols every second and hands us fresh data. Dashboard.jsx owns the state: the list of rows, the current filter text, the sort key, and the selected symbol. I wrote this version badly, deliberately. State lives too high, everything is recomputed on every render, and nothing is memoized. So when I run it and type in the search box, watch what happens.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Dashboard That Lags on Purpose
text: I type a single letter into the filter, and the input stutters. There's a visible delay between the key press and the character appearing. That is the bug we're hunting, and it's a very real kind of bug. Nothing is throwing an error, nothing is broken functionally, the table is correct. It's just slow, and slow is a feature users feel before they can describe it. Now, you might already have guesses about why. Maybe it's the filtering, maybe it's five thousand rows rendering, maybe it's the timer. Hold on to those guesses, because one of the lessons of this course is that guessing about performance is usually wrong, and that's why chapter two is entirely about profiling.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Dashboard That Lags on Purpose
text: Here's the road map. Chapter one is fundamentals: what React does when it renders, what actually triggers a re-render, and how React compares props. Chapter two is the React DevTools Profiler, where we find the wasted work. Chapter three is state placement and useMemo for computed data. Chapter four is React.memo and useCallback, plus the traps that quietly break them. Chapter five is rendering less, with virtualization and useTransition. And chapter six is where we profile the fixed dashboard and compare against today's numbers. You only need to be comfortable with components, props, state and hooks. Clone the starter project, run it, and type in that filter box so you feel the lag yourself. See you in the next lecture.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Render vs Commit: What React Actually Does
text: Before we optimize anything we need a precise picture of what React does when we say a component renders. This is where a lot of confusion starts, because the word render gets used for two completely different things. In this lecture I'll separate them: the render phase and the commit phase. Once you can hold those two in your head, a lot of performance advice suddenly makes sense, and a lot of folk wisdom turns out to be wrong. We'll use our dashboard as the example, so open Dashboard.jsx and PriceRow.jsx next to each other, because we'll keep jumping between them.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Render vs Commit: What React Actually Does
text: Start with the render phase. When React renders a component, all it does is call your function. That's it. Our PriceRow function runs, it reads its props, and it returns a description of what the UI should look like, which is a tree of plain objects we call React elements. Nothing has touched the browser yet. No DOM nodes were created, no text changed on screen. Rendering is just computing a description. That's why it's supposed to be pure: same props and state in, same description out. And notice that this means a render can be wasted. If PriceRow runs and returns exactly the description it returned last time, React did real work, your function body, for nothing.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Render vs Commit: What React Actually Does
text: Now the commit phase. After the render phase, React compares the new description with the previous one. This comparison is what people call reconciliation, or diffing. React walks the two trees, figures out the smallest set of changes, and only then it commits: it actually updates the DOM, changes the text node, sets the attribute, and runs layout effects. So here's the key idea. A component can render without anything being committed. If PriceRow renders but its price is still 101.25, the diff finds no difference, and the DOM is left completely alone. The browser does zero work. But your JavaScript still ran, and with five thousand rows, that JavaScript adds up fast.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Render vs Commit: What React Actually Does
text: Let me make this concrete in the code. In PriceRow.jsx I'll add a console log at the top of the function: `console.log('render', symbol)`. I'll also open the Elements panel in the browser and turn on paint flashing so I can see DOM updates. Now I type in the filter box. The console floods with render messages, thousands of them, but the paint flashing shows only a few rows actually repaint. That gap is the whole story. Lots of renders, very few commits. The renders are pure overhead, JavaScript running to confirm that nothing changed. Our goal for the rest of this course is to close that gap, so React only calls the components whose output could actually be different.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Render vs Commit: What React Actually Does
text: One more thing, and it's a common misunderstanding. A render does not mean the DOM was rebuilt. React is not throwing away your page on every state change, and you shouldn't be afraid of renders as such. Renders are usually cheap. The trouble is when they're expensive, or when there are far too many of them, like our five thousand rows. So the question to ask is never how do I avoid all renders, it's how do I avoid the renders that don't change anything. Keep the console log in PriceRow, we'll lean on it, and in the next lecture we'll look at the exact events that cause React to start a render in the first place.

lecture_title: 1.3 - What Triggers a Re-render
text: Let's answer the question that sits underneath everything in this course: what makes React re-render a component? If you can't answer that precisely, you'll end up memoizing the wrong things. And there's a very short list of triggers. I'll go through them one at a time and prove each one in the dashboard, using the console log we left in PriceRow. Open Dashboard.jsx, because most of what we'll talk about happens there. I'm going to try to convince you of one sentence that you should memorize, and then we'll spend the lecture seeing why it's true.

lecture_title: 1.3 - What Triggers a Re-render
text: The first trigger is state. When a component calls its setter, say `setFilter`, React schedules a re-render of that component. The second trigger is context: when a value provided by a context provider changes, every component that reads that context re-renders. The third is a parent re-render. And here's the sentence. When a component renders, React renders all of its children, recursively, whether or not their props changed. That's the default behavior. Props changing is not a trigger at all. It's a common myth that a child re-renders because its props changed. It re-renders because its parent rendered. Props only matter once we opt in to checking them, which we'll do with React.memo later.

lecture_title: 1.3 - What Triggers a Re-render
text: Let's prove it. In Dashboard.jsx we have `const [filter, setFilter] = useState('')`, and we pass `filter` to the FilterBar and also use it to compute the visible rows. The PriceTable receives `rows` as a prop and maps over them to render a PriceRow for each. Now I'll type one character. `setFilter` runs, Dashboard re-renders, so PriceTable re-renders, so every single PriceRow re-renders, even the ones whose symbol and price are exactly the same as before. Look at the console. Five thousand log lines for a single keystroke. The rows didn't ask for any of that. Their parent simply rendered, and the default is to keep going down the tree.

lecture_title: 1.3 - What Triggers a Re-render
text: A second example is the live feed. The useTicks hook calls `setPrices` every second with a few hundred updated symbols. That state lives in Dashboard too. So every tick re-renders Dashboard, then the table, then all five thousand rows, even though only a few hundred prices actually changed. Do you see the pattern? State sits high in the tree, which means any change to it re-renders everything beneath. That's not a React bug. It's the design. React assumes renders are cheap and correctness matters more. Our job is to give it hints, through where we put state and through memoization, so it can skip the pointless work.

lecture_title: 1.3 - What Triggers a Re-render
text: A few myths to clear up before we move on. Changing a ref does not trigger a re-render. A variable you reassign inside a component does not trigger one either. And calling a setter with the same value you already have usually bails out, though React may still render that one component once more before it bails. So the short list is: state, context, and parent renders. That's it. In the next lecture we'll look at how React decides whether two values are the same, because that comparison, shallow equality, is the mechanism behind almost every optimization we'll use, and also behind most of the ways they fail.

lecture_title: 1.4 - Shallow Equality: How React Compares Props and State
text: This lecture is about one small idea that causes a huge share of real-world React performance bugs: shallow equality. Whenever React needs to ask whether something changed, whether that's a state update, a dependency array, or a memoized component's props, it uses basically the same check. It compares values with `Object.is`. If you understand exactly what that comparison does and does not look at, you can predict when memoization will work and when it will silently do nothing. We'll do a few experiments in a scratch file, so create one called equality.js and follow along.

lecture_title: 1.4 - Shallow Equality: How React Compares Props and State
text: Start with primitives. `Object.is(5, 5)` is true. `Object.is('AAPL', 'AAPL')` is true. Numbers, strings, booleans compare by value, so two separate 101.25s are equal. Now objects. I'll write `const a = { price: 101.25 }` and `const b = { price: 101.25 }`, then `Object.is(a, b)`. That prints false. Same contents, but they're two different objects living at two different places in memory. Equality for objects, arrays and functions means same reference, not same contents. `Object.is(a, a)` is true, of course. Keep this in your head, because everything in the next three chapters is a story about references.

lecture_title: 1.4 - Shallow Equality: How React Compares Props and State
text: Now what does shallow mean? When React.memo compares props, it takes the old props object and the new props object, and for each key it runs `Object.is` on the old value and the new value. It only goes one level deep. It doesn't look inside an object prop to compare its fields. So if a PriceRow receives `price={101.25}` and `symbol='AAPL'`, both primitives, that's a cheap and reliable comparison. But if it receives `quote={{ price: 101.25 }}` and the parent builds that object literal during every render, the reference is new every time, the shallow check says changed, and the component re-renders even though nothing meaningful changed.

lecture_title: 1.4 - Shallow Equality: How React Compares Props and State
text: Here's where it bites in the dashboard. In Dashboard.jsx I compute `const visibleRows = rows.filter(r => r.symbol.includes(filter))`. Every render, `filter` creates a brand-new array. The contents might be identical, but the reference is new. So any memoized component receiving visibleRows would see a changed prop every time. The same goes for `const onSelect = (symbol) => setSelected(symbol)`, a new function on every render. Functions are objects too. And dependency arrays work the same way: useEffect and useMemo compare each dependency with `Object.is`, so an object dependency created inline will re-run the effect every single render.

lecture_title: 1.4 - Shallow Equality: How React Compares Props and State
text: So here's the model to carry forward. React does cheap reference checks, not deep comparisons, because deep comparison of big data would itself be expensive. That means our job as developers is to keep references stable when the data hasn't changed: keep the same array, the same object, the same function. Two tools help: useMemo for values and useCallback for functions. We'll build both properly in chapters three and four. But first, in chapter two, we're going to stop theorizing and use the Profiler to see which components are actually rendering for nothing in our dashboard. Make sure you can explain why those two identical objects aren't equal.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Profiling the Dashboard with React DevTools
text: Time to stop guessing and measure. In this lecture we'll use the React DevTools Profiler on our dashboard. If you don't have the React Developer Tools browser extension installed, add it now for Chrome or Firefox. After you install it, open the dashboard, open your browser DevTools, and you'll see two new tabs: Components and Profiler. We'll use Profiler. One important setup note: profile a development build for learning, since it gives you component names and warnings, but remember that production is faster, so treat absolute numbers as relative, and compare before against after on the same machine.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Profiling the Dashboard with React DevTools
text: Here's the workflow. In the Profiler tab there's a round record button. Before you click it, click the gear icon and turn on the option to record why each component rendered. That setting is the most useful one in the whole tool. Now press record, perform exactly one action, and press stop. I'll type a single letter into the filter box, then stop. The discipline matters here: one interaction per recording, otherwise you can't tell which work belongs to which action. If you record for ten seconds of random clicking, you'll get a pile of data you can't interpret.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Profiling the Dashboard with React DevTools
text: Now we have a commit chart at the top. Each bar is one commit, one time React actually committed changes to the DOM, and its height and color show how long it took. Our single keystroke produced a tall yellow bar, around ninety milliseconds on my machine. For a smooth interface you want work per interaction under about sixteen milliseconds, since that's one frame at sixty frames per second. Ninety is more than five frames, which is exactly why the input feels sticky. Write that number down. This is our baseline: ninety milliseconds for one keystroke in the filter. Everything we do from here has to push that number down, and we'll check it each time.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Profiling the Dashboard with React DevTools
text: Click on that bar and the flame graph below shows the component tree for that commit. Each rectangle is a component, wide means it took more time, and the color tells you whether it rendered. Gray components didn't render in this commit. Colored ones did. Hover over PriceRow and the tooltip tells us the render time and, because we turned on the setting, why it rendered. For almost every row it says the parent component rendered. That confirms what we reasoned in chapter one: the rows render only because Dashboard did. Nothing about the rows themselves changed. We now have evidence rather than a hunch.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Profiling the Dashboard with React DevTools
text: There's also a ranked view, which sorts components by how long they took, slowest first. That's useful when one expensive component hides among thousands of cheap ones. In our case the ranked chart shows a wall of PriceRow entries, each tiny, but five thousand of them. Death by a thousand cuts, literally five thousand. That's the shape of problem we have. In the next lecture we'll read the flame graph more carefully, learn to tell useful renders from wasted ones, and build a short list of suspects. Before you move on, record your own baseline for one keystroke and keep the number.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Reading the Flame Graph for Wasted Renders
text: In the last lecture we recorded a baseline. Now we'll learn to read the flame graph for wasted renders, because that's the skill that tells you what to fix and, just as important, what to leave alone. A wasted render is one where the component's function ran and produced the same output as before. The Profiler can't say that directly in one click, but it gives us strong clues. We'll walk through a recording of the dashboard while a price tick arrives, not a keystroke this time, so we can see how the live feed behaves differently from the filter.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Reading the Flame Graph for Wasted Renders
text: I record one price tick from useTicks and stop. In the flame graph, the top component is App, then Dashboard, then FilterBar and PriceTable. Look at FilterBar. It rendered, shown in color. Why? The tooltip says the parent component rendered. But nothing about the filter changed. The filter box didn't care about a price tick, yet it re-ran. That's a cheap component so it doesn't matter much, and this is the first lesson: not every wasted render deserves a fix. Use the ranked view to focus on cost. A wasted render that takes zero point one milliseconds is noise. Five thousand of them are not.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Reading the Flame Graph for Wasted Renders
text: Now PriceTable and its PriceRow children. A tick updates a few hundred symbols. So for those few hundred rows, a render is legitimate, their price changed. But look at the flame graph: all five thousand rows are colored. The other four thousand seven hundred rendered for nothing. The Profiler's why-did-this-render tooltip tells us the same thing for each of them: parent rendered, props unchanged. That's the pattern to look for: a long run of identical siblings, all colored, all blamed on the parent. In our dashboard that is the single biggest cost, and it's what memoization will eventually address.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Reading the Flame Graph for Wasted Renders
text: Let's look at a different kind of clue: components that render much more often than you'd expect. Use the commit chart to step through several commits with the arrow keys, and watch which components light up each time. I see Dashboard in every commit, that's expected, it owns the state. But PriceTable also computes the visible rows by filtering and sorting five thousand items, on every commit, even a tick that doesn't change the sort order of anything the user cares about. In the ranked view that shows up as a single fat bar rather than a thousand thin ones. Thin and many means memoize children. Fat and single means avoid recomputing.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Reading the Flame Graph for Wasted Renders
text: So after this lecture we have a suspect list with evidence. One, state in Dashboard is too high, so everything beneath re-renders on every tick and keystroke. Two, the filter and sort computation runs every render. Three, the five thousand PriceRow components render regardless of whether their data changed. Four, inline functions and objects passed down probably defeat any memoization we add, but we'll verify that when we get there. Notice that these map directly to the next chapters. Chapter three handles one and two, chapter four handles three and four. Make a note of your own suspect list, and let's start fixing, beginning with where state lives.

lecture_title: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up
text: Our first real fix is the one that costs the least and often delivers the most: put state where it's used. Before we reach for any memoization hook, we should ask whether the state is in the right place at all. Remember the rule from chapter one: when a component re-renders, all its children re-render. So state held high up makes a large subtree re-render. If we move the state down into a smaller component, only that small subtree re-renders when it changes. Let's open Dashboard.jsx and see where the filter state lives right now.

lecture_title: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up
text: Currently `const [filter, setFilter] = useState('')` lives in Dashboard, right next to rows and the selected symbol. The filter is used in two places: the FilterBar, which shows the text input, and the visible row computation. Every keystroke calls setFilter, which re-renders Dashboard, which re-renders the table and its five thousand rows. Now, in this case the filter is genuinely needed by both the input and the table, so we can't just push it down into FilterBar. But there's another piece of state in Dashboard that is not shared: `hoveredSymbol`, used only by a small tooltip. That one is a perfect candidate to move down.

lecture_title: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up
text: Let's do it. I'll create a new component called SymbolTooltip in its own file. I cut `const [hovered, setHovered] = useState(null)` out of Dashboard and paste it into SymbolTooltip, along with the mouse handlers that set it. Now when the user hovers, only SymbolTooltip re-renders. The five thousand rows are untouched, because they aren't children of SymbolTooltip. Let me record this in the Profiler: hover over a row. Before the change the commit was sixty milliseconds, and now it's under two. That is a thirty-fold improvement without a single useMemo, only by moving a line of code.

lecture_title: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up
text: The second technique is lifting content up, which sounds like the opposite but is the same idea. Suppose we have a component that holds some state and wraps expensive children. For example, a ResizablePanel with a `width` state that wraps our PriceTable. When the width changes, the panel re-renders, and so does the table, because the table is rendered inside the panel's function. But if instead Dashboard renders the table and passes it as `children` to the panel, the table element is created by Dashboard, not by the panel. When the panel's state changes, React sees the same children element reference and skips it.

lecture_title: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up
text: This works because of what we learned about references. The children prop is an element object created in the parent. When the panel re-renders because of its own state, that prop is the same reference as before, so React doesn't need to re-render it. So the rule of thumb: first try to move state down to the component that needs it, and when a stateful wrapper surrounds slow content, pass the content in as children. These cost nothing, they have no dependency arrays to maintain, and they can't go stale. Only after that do we reach for memoization, which is exactly what we'll do in the next lecture. Re-record the hover interaction and write down your new number.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Memoization and Computed State
text: We moved state down, and that fixed the hover. Now let's deal with suspect number two, the filter and sort computation. Open Dashboard.jsx again. Right now, in the body of the component, we have `const visibleRows = rows.filter(r => r.symbol.includes(filter)).sort(compareBy(sortKey))`. That runs top to bottom on every render of Dashboard, and Dashboard renders on every price tick, every keystroke, and every selection change. Filtering five thousand rows and then sorting what's left is real work. Let me show you how much, using a little `console.time` around it, before we change anything.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Memoization and Computed State
text: I wrap the line with `console.time('visible')` and `console.timeEnd('visible')`, and then I trigger a price tick. The console says visible took about eleven milliseconds. Not terrible alone, but it runs on every tick, even when the filter and sort key are exactly what they were a second ago. Same inputs, same output, computed again. That's the situation memoization exists for. So before I write any code, let me explain what memoization is, because the word sounds fancier than it is. It's remembering. And React gives us a hook for it.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Memoization and Computed State
text: Memoization is an optimization technique where you cache the result of an expensive computation and return the cached result when the same inputs occur again instead of recomputing. In React, useMemo lets you memoize the result of a computation and only recompute it when its dependencies change. This is particularly valuable for computed state that derives from props or other state values and would otherwise be recalculated on every render even when the inputs have not changed. So that's the idea in the abstract. Now let's apply it to visibleRows, and I want you to notice what the inputs are: the rows array, the filter string, and the sort key. If none of those three changed, we should reuse the previous result. Those three values are our dependencies.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Memoization and Computed State
text: Here's the code. I'll write `const visibleRows = useMemo(() => { return rows.filter(r => r.symbol.includes(filter)).sort(compareBy(sortKey)) }, [rows, filter, sortKey])`. The first argument is the function that does the computation, and the second is the dependency array. React runs the function on the first render and stores the result. On later renders it compares each dependency to the previous one with `Object.is`, the shallow check from chapter one, and if they're all the same it returns the stored result without calling the function. I'll save and tick again. The console now shows the visible computation only when rows actually changes, and hovering or selecting no longer triggers it at all.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Memoization and Computed State
text: useMemo and useCallback are both memoization hooks but they serve different purposes. useMemo memoizes a computed value while useCallback memoizes a function reference. You need useCallback when you pass callbacks to child components that are themselves wrapped in React.memo, because without memoizing the callback the child still re-renders since it receives a new function reference on every parent render. The combination of React.memo on the child component and useCallback on the parent's callback prop is the complete pattern for preventing unnecessary child renders. Notice that second half especially, because it connects to the reference equality we've been building up since chapter one. We'll spend the whole next chapter on exactly that pattern, so for now just remember that useMemo handles values and useCallback handles functions.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Memoization and Computed State
text: Memoization helps computed state because it prevents redundant work during renders. If you have a filtered and sorted list derived from a large array of items, and the filter or sort criteria have not changed, there is no reason to redo that work. Without useMemo the filter and sort run on every render even when unrelated state updates trigger a re-render. With useMemo the computation is skipped entirely if the dependencies have not changed. The main pitfall is over-memoizing: adding useMemo everywhere without profiling first adds overhead from the dependency comparison that can actually be slower than just recomputing. Let's make that concrete with our dashboard. I removed the console.time wrappers, and the visible rows computation is now skipped on every render where its inputs are unchanged. One caution before we move on. A new rows array arrives with every tick, so on a tick the memo still recomputes, because rows changed. That's correct behavior. Memoization only saves work when the inputs truly stayed the same, and in the next lecture we'll look at when it isn't worth it at all.

lecture_title: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves
text: Last lecture we added useMemo, and it's tempting now to wrap everything in it. Please don't. In this lecture I want to show you the cases where useMemo costs more than it saves, because knowing when not to use a tool is half of using it well. Every useMemo call has a price. React has to store the previous value and the dependency array, and on every render it has to compare each dependency. Plus, you've made your code harder to read, and every future reader has to check that dependency list. That price is small, but if the thing you're memoizing is cheaper than the price, you've made things slower. So let's measure instead of guessing.

lecture_title: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves
text: Let me add a small example to Dashboard.jsx. Suppose I compute `const totalVolume = rows.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.volume, 0)` to show in the header. It looks like work, five thousand additions. So I wrap it in useMemo with `[rows]` as the dependency. Now let's profile both versions. Without useMemo, the reduce takes about point three milliseconds. With useMemo, on a tick the dependency changed anyway, since rows is a new array every tick, so the reduce runs again, plus React did the dependency comparison and the bookkeeping. We've paid extra for a cache that never hits.

lecture_title: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves
text: That's the first trap: a memo whose dependencies change on nearly every render is pure overhead. A cache only helps when it hits. The second trap is memoizing something trivial. Concatenating two strings, doing a few additions, building a tiny object, those take microseconds, less than the comparison cost. A useful rule of thumb from the React docs is to measure with `console.time`, and if the calculation takes a millisecond or more, consider memoizing it. You can even simulate a slower device by throttling the CPU in browser DevTools, to see which calculations would hurt on a phone.

lecture_title: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves
text: The third trap is the one that bites in real codebases: stale or wrong dependencies. If I write `useMemo(() => rows.filter(r => r.symbol.includes(filter)), [rows])` and forget `filter`, the list stops updating when the user types, because React thinks nothing relevant changed. The ESLint rule `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` catches this, so make sure you have it turned on, and don't silence it with a comment. A memoization bug is worse than a performance problem, since it gives you wrong output. And that's the point: every useMemo adds a promise you must keep up, that the dependency list is correct.

lecture_title: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves
text: So here's my decision procedure. First, can I fix this by moving state down or restructuring? Do that. Second, is the computation measurably slow, say a millisecond or more, and do its inputs often stay the same? Then use useMemo. Otherwise, skip it. In our dashboard, visibleRows passes both tests, and totalVolume fails both, so I'll remove that useMemo. We've now handled suspects one and two. Next chapter we get to the big one: the five thousand rows re-rendering for nothing, and the tools for that are React.memo and useCallback. Re-profile your keystroke before moving on.

lecture_title: 4.1 - React.memo and useCallback
text: Now we reach the part of the dashboard that hurts the most: five thousand PriceRow components re-rendering when only a few hundred prices changed. This is exactly what React.memo is for. Welcome to chapter four. In the Profiler we saw every row colored, blamed on the parent, with identical props. React.memo lets a component say, if my props are the same as last time, don't call me. So let's open PriceRow.jsx, where we have a plain function component that takes `symbol`, `price`, `change`, `volume`, and an `onSelect` callback, and see what happens when we wrap it.

lecture_title: 4.1 - React.memo and useCallback
text: By default a React component re-renders whenever its parent re-renders, even if its props did not change. React.memo wraps a component and skips the re-render when its props are shallowly equal to the previous render. The catch is shallow equality: primitives compare by value, but objects, arrays, and functions compare by reference. If a parent creates a new function or object literal on every render and passes it as a prop, React.memo sees a brand-new reference each time and re-renders anyway, defeating the optimization. Let's see that in our own code. I'll change the export in PriceRow.jsx to `export default React.memo(PriceRow)`. That's the entire change. Now save, record a single price tick in the Profiler, and look at the flame graph.

lecture_title: 4.1 - React.memo and useCallback
text: I expected the gray wall of skipped rows, and it's not there. Most rows are still colored, and the tooltip now says that the props changed, specifically `onSelect`. This is the reference trap we've been warning about since chapter one. In PriceTable.jsx, I map over the rows and write `<PriceRow key={r.symbol} {...r} onSelect={(s) => setSelected(s)} />`. That arrow function is created fresh on every render of the table. Same behavior, but a new function object each time, so the shallow comparison inside React.memo sees a changed prop for every single row and re-renders all of them. We added memo and got no benefit.

lecture_title: 4.1 - React.memo and useCallback
text: useCallback and useMemo exist to keep references stable across renders. useCallback returns the same function instance as long as its dependency array does not change, and useMemo does the same for a computed value. Wrapping a callback in useCallback before passing it to a React.memo child means the child actually sees a stable prop and can skip re-rendering. The rule of thumb: memoizing is only worth it when the child is expensive to render or the reference is consumed by a memoized child — wrapping everything adds overhead and dependency bugs for no benefit. So let's do exactly that. In Dashboard.jsx I'll write `const handleSelect = useCallback((symbol) => { setSelected(symbol) }, [])`. The dependency array is empty, because `setSelected` from useState is guaranteed to be stable, and we only use the symbol argument. Then I pass `onSelect={handleSelect}` down through PriceTable to each row. Now handleSelect is the same function instance on every render of Dashboard.

lecture_title: 4.1 - React.memo and useCallback
text: Save, record a tick, and look. Now the flame graph is mostly gray. Only the rows whose price actually changed are colored, a few hundred instead of five thousand. The commit that took ninety milliseconds drops to about eighteen. That's our first big, measured win in the main interaction. Check the keystroke too: typing in the filter now re-renders only the rows that enter or leave the visible list. Two things to remember. React.memo does nothing alone if the props contain fresh references. And useCallback does nothing alone if the child isn't memoized. They work as a pair, and next lecture we'll hunt the other ways to break that pair.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo
text: We got memo working on PriceRow, but I want to be honest that it was fragile. One careless line anywhere in the chain and the entire optimization silently turns off, and nothing warns you. React will not tell you that memo is being defeated. So in this lecture we'll go looking for the most common culprits: inline objects, inline arrays, and inline functions passed as props. We'll deliberately break our own fix, watch the Profiler catch it, and then learn the habits that prevent it. Open PriceTable.jsx and PriceRow.jsx side by side.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo
text: Let me add a feature that seems innocent. Each row needs a little style tweak depending on whether it's selected, so in PriceTable I write `<PriceRow key={r.symbol} {...r} style={{ color: r.change > 0 ? 'green' : 'red' }} onSelect={handleSelect} />`. Looks harmless, right? But the double curly braces mean an object literal, created fresh during every render of the table. New object, new reference, so shallow equality fails and memo re-renders every row again. I'll record a tick in the Profiler to confirm, and yes, the wall of colored rows is back, with the tooltip pointing to the style prop.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo
text: There are a few ways out. The best one is not to pass an object at all. Pass primitives. Instead of a style object, pass `change={r.change}` and let PriceRow compute the color itself inside, since it already receives change as a number. Primitives compare by value, so memo works naturally. The second option is to hoist constants. If the object never changes, define it outside the component, like `const GREEN = { color: 'green' }`, so it's created once at module load and the reference is stable forever. The third option is useMemo for objects that really depend on props or state.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo
text: The same applies to arrays and to functions that need arguments. Suppose each row has a remove button and we write `onRemove={() => removeSymbol(r.symbol)}`. That closure is new for each row on each render. A tidy fix is to pass the stable function and the symbol separately: `onRemove={removeSymbol}` along with the symbol, which the row already has, and then inside PriceRow the click handler calls `onRemove(symbol)`. Now the prop is the same function every time, and the child supplies its own argument. That pattern, stable callback plus data the child already knows, removes the need for per-row closures.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo
text: Another subtle trap is the children prop. If you pass JSX as children to a memoized component, like `hi`, that JSX creates a new element object every render, so a memoized Card will re-render anyway. Same story: new reference. And the debugging approach is always the same. Record in the Profiler with the why-rendered setting on, look at which prop the tooltip blames, and find where that prop is created. A tip: React DevTools highlights memoized components with a Memo badge, which helps you confirm memo is actually applied. Next lecture, the most sneaky trap of all, context.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms
text: There's one more way to defeat memoization, and it's the sneakiest, because React.memo cannot stop it at all: context. In this lecture we'll look at a re-render storm caused by context, and then fix it by splitting the context into pieces. Here's the setup. Our dashboard has a DashboardContext provided in App.jsx. It holds the selected symbol, the current filter, the user's watchlist, and the theme. Components deep in the tree, including PriceRow, read from it with `useContext(DashboardContext)`, because passing these through props felt tedious. And now we'll see the cost.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms
text: The key fact: when a context value changes, every component that calls useContext for that context re-renders, regardless of React.memo. Memo only guards against re-renders caused by a parent. A context update goes straight to the consumers. In PriceRow I read `const { theme, selected } = useContext(DashboardContext)`. Now someone types in the filter, the provider value changes, and since all five thousand rows consume the context, all five thousand re-render, memo or not. I'll record the keystroke and confirm: the tooltip says context changed, and our memo wall is gone again.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms
text: Why did the value change? In App.jsx the provider says `<DashboardContext.Provider value={{ selected, filter, watchlist, theme }}>`. That object literal is created on every render of App, so even a change to something unrelated produces a new object. And any change to any field, say filter, means every consumer sees a new value, even consumers that only use theme. Context has no selector. A consumer can't say that it only cares about one field. If you read the context, you re-render when any part of its value changes.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms
text: The fix is to split the context by how often things change and who needs them. I'll make a ThemeContext holding only `theme`, a SelectionContext for `selected`, and a FilterContext for `filter`. The rows only need theme and selection, so they subscribe to those two and never see filter changes. The filter context is consumed only by FilterBar and the table. I also memoize each provider value with useMemo, so the value only changes when its actual contents change, for example `useMemo(() => ({ selected, setSelected }), [selected])`. Now typing in the filter no longer touches the rows.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms
text: Another approach is to separate state from the functions that update it. Setters are stable, so put them in their own context, like SelectionDispatchContext, and components that only trigger changes will never re-render when the state changes. Let's check the result. Record the keystroke again and compare: the five thousand re-renders are down to the rows entering or leaving the filtered list. Quick summary of the rule. Keep context values small and focused, memoize provider values, and split by update frequency. If you need fine-grained subscription to a big store, look at libraries with selectors, but for most dashboards, splitting contexts is enough. Next up, rendering less.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Virtualizing the 5,000-Row Table
text: We've cut the wasted renders, but there's still a fundamental problem we haven't touched: we're rendering five thousand rows into the DOM, when the screen shows about twenty. No amount of memoization changes that the browser must create and lay out five thousand table rows, and that has a real cost on first load and on every filter change. The fix is virtualization, sometimes called windowing: render only the rows that are visible, plus a small buffer, and fake the rest. Let's implement it in PriceTable.jsx. Open the Profiler first to see the commit time when the filter clears and all five thousand rows mount.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Virtualizing the 5,000-Row Table
text: The baseline: clearing the filter takes about three hundred milliseconds, mostly mounting thousands of DOM nodes. Memo can't help here, since these are new mounts, not re-renders. Here's the idea. The table container has a fixed height, say six hundred pixels, and `overflow: auto`. Each row is a fixed height, say thirty-two pixels. So the total scrollable height is five thousand times thirty-two, one hundred sixty thousand pixels. We render one tall empty div with that height, so the scrollbar behaves as if all rows existed. Then we render only the rows whose position falls inside the visible window, absolutely positioned at the correct offset.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Virtualizing the 5,000-Row Table
text: Let me write the core math. We track `scrollTop` in state, updated from the container's onScroll handler. The first visible index is `Math.floor(scrollTop / ROW_HEIGHT)`. The number of visible rows is `Math.ceil(containerHeight / ROW_HEIGHT)`. We add an overscan, a few extra rows above and below, say five, so scrolling fast doesn't show blank gaps. Then `const visible = rows.slice(start, end)`. For each one, I render a PriceRow with `style={{ position: 'absolute', top: index * ROW_HEIGHT }}`. Note that the style object here is inline again, so I'll compute the offset inside the row from an `index` prop instead, to keep memo working.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Virtualizing the 5,000-Row Table
text: In practice you'd probably use a library like react-window or TanStack Virtual, which handle edge cases such as variable heights, resize observers, and keyboard accessibility. I'm writing the core by hand so you understand what these libraries do, but for production, use the library. With react-window it looks like a `FixedSizeList` with `height`, `itemCount`, `itemSize`, and a row component that receives an `index` and a `style` prop. One more point: the library gives you a style object per row, and that's fine because it caches them, so memo still works when you wrap your row in React.memo.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Virtualizing the 5,000-Row Table
text: Now the measurements. After virtualization, the DOM contains about thirty rows instead of five thousand. Clearing the filter takes under ten milliseconds. Scrolling stays smooth because we mount and unmount only a handful of rows per frame. A price tick re-renders only the visible rows whose prices changed, maybe three or four. There are trade-offs, though. Browser find-in-page can't see rows that aren't in the DOM, and screen reader users lose some context, so add aria attributes like the total row count. Virtualization is powerful but not free, which is why we did it after the cheap fixes. Next: keeping typing responsive with useTransition.

lecture_title: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering
text: Our table is cheap to render now, but there's one more problem I want to address, and it's about priority. When the user types in the filter, two things happen: the input's text must update right away, and the table must update to show the matching rows. If the table update is expensive, it can block the input from updating, and the typing feels laggy. But the input matters more than the table, and the table could wait a few milliseconds. React 18 gives us tools to say so. They're useTransition and useDeferredValue, and we'll use both in the dashboard.

lecture_title: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering
text: Start with useTransition. I'll open Dashboard.jsx and import it. `const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()`. Currently the input's onChange does `setFilter(e.target.value)`, and that single state drives both the input value and the heavy table. I'll split it into two pieces of state. `inputValue` is the urgent one, bound directly to the input. `filter` is the one that drives the table. In the handler I write `setInputValue(value)` right away, then `startTransition(() => { setFilter(value) })`. The first update is urgent and renders immediately. The second is marked as a transition, a low-priority update.

lecture_title: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering
text: What does React do with a transition? It renders the transition update in the background, and if a more urgent update arrives, say the next keystroke, React interrupts the in-progress render, throws it away, and handles the urgent one first. This is why the input stays responsive even when the table rendering is slow. It's concurrent rendering. Also, `isPending` is true while the transition is in progress, so I can dim the table slightly, `opacity: isPending ? 0.6 : 1`, to show the user that results are catching up. The keystroke itself now commits in about two milliseconds, even when the table update lags behind.

lecture_title: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering
text: Now useDeferredValue, which is the same idea from the other direction. Sometimes you don't own the code that sets the state, for example the value comes from a prop. Then you can write `const deferredFilter = useDeferredValue(filter)` and use `deferredFilter` to compute the visible rows. React first renders with the old deferred value, so the urgent update finishes fast, then re-renders in the background with the new one. I'd use useTransition when I control the setter, and useDeferredValue when I only receive a value. For the dashboard, either works, and I'll keep the transition, since it also gives us isPending.

lecture_title: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering
text: One important caveat. These tools don't make the work faster, they make the app feel faster by prioritizing. The total render work is the same, or even slightly more if renders are interrupted and restarted. That's why we did the real optimizations first, and why we use transitions last, for the work that is still genuinely slow. Also, transitions only wrap state updates, not timers or fetches, and updates inside a transition can't be used to control a text input directly, which is why we kept inputValue separate. Next chapter, we'll measure everything together and compare against our baseline.

lecture_title: 6.1 - Before and After: Profiling the Fixed Dashboard
text: It's time to close the loop. We started this course with a dashboard that took ninety milliseconds to handle a single keystroke, and we promised to measure every change. In this lecture we profile the fixed dashboard, and compare it against that baseline. Let's open the app, open the React DevTools Profiler, turn on record-why-rendered, and repeat exactly the same interaction we recorded in lecture two: type one letter into the filter box. Same machine, same browser, same data, same development build. If you change the conditions, the comparison means nothing, so be strict about that.

lecture_title: 6.1 - Before and After: Profiling the Fixed Dashboard
text: I stop the recording and look at the commit chart. The bar that was ninety milliseconds yellow is now a short blue bar, around four milliseconds. In the flame graph, the FilterBar rendered, the table rendered with a handful of visible rows, and almost everything else is gray. The tooltip for the visible rows says the props changed, because those rows are legitimately showing different data. That's what a healthy profile looks like: components render when there's a reason and stay gray when there isn't. We went from ninety to four, over twenty times faster, and no single trick got us there.

lecture_title: 6.1 - Before and After: Profiling the Fixed Dashboard
text: Let me list what contributed. Moving the hover state into SymbolTooltip cut that interaction from sixty milliseconds to two. useMemo on the visible rows skipped the filter and sort when inputs hadn't changed. React.memo on PriceRow plus useCallback for handleSelect took a tick from ninety to eighteen. Fixing the inline style object and splitting the context kept memo working. Virtualization cut mounting from five thousand rows to about thirty. And useTransition kept typing responsive. It's worth running a little experiment: turn each fix off one at a time and see which number moves. That tells you which fix pays the rent.

lecture_title: 6.1 - Before and After: Profiling the Fixed Dashboard
text: Now let's try the stress test, the one that matters. I'll throttle the CPU to six times slower in the browser's Performance panel, which approximates a mid-range phone, and type quickly. The input stays responsive and the table catches up a moment later, dimmed while pending. On the original version the page froze for over half a second per keystroke under the same throttling. This is also a good habit for you: always check performance on a slow profile, not only on your fast laptop, because users don't all have your hardware.

lecture_title: 6.1 - Before and After: Profiling the Fixed Dashboard
text: A few honest caveats. First, development mode in React is slower than production, so run a production build and profile that too, using the Profiler build if you want numbers. Second, I'd keep a performance budget, a number like sixteen milliseconds per interaction, and re-check it when the codebase grows, because optimizations rot. Third, don't forget that these fixes added complexity: dependency arrays, memo boundaries, split contexts. Each one is a maintenance cost. So write down why each exists, ideally in a comment pointing to the measurement. In the final lecture, let's talk about where you can go from here.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Where from Here?
text: Congratulations, you made it to the end of React Performance Patterns. Let's take a few minutes to step back, summarize what we did, and talk about where to go from here. We started with a trading dashboard that was deliberately slow, a five thousand row price table that stuttered on every keystroke and every live tick. We profiled it with the React DevTools Profiler, found the wasted work, and fixed it one measured change at a time. Along the way you learned the concepts underneath the fixes, and I think those matter more than the specific code.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Where from Here?
text: Let me restate the mental model in a few sentences. A render is calling your function, and a commit is touching the DOM. Components re-render because of state, context, or because their parent rendered, never simply because props changed. React compares props and dependencies with shallow reference checks, which means that keeping references stable is the central skill. Moving state down and lifting content up are free fixes. useMemo caches expensive derived values. React.memo and useCallback work as a pair. Inline objects, functions and context values quietly break them. And virtualization and transitions handle what's left.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Where from Here?
text: The workflow matters more than any single hook. Measure first with a baseline, form a hypothesis from the Profiler, change one thing, and measure again. If a change doesn't move the number, remove it. This protects you from the most common failure in performance work, which is cluttering a codebase with optimizations that do nothing and make future changes harder. Remember our totalVolume example, where useMemo made things slightly worse. Evidence beats intuition, including mine, so try the techniques from this course on your own projects and see which ones actually show up in your profiles.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Where from Here?
text: Here's what I'd suggest as next steps. First, take the dashboard and extend it: add a second table with sparklines, or a column that does a heavier computation, and profile what breaks. Second, read about React Compiler, which aims to apply memoization automatically at build time; understanding the manual patterns in this course will help you know what it does for you and where it can't. Third, explore tools such as why-did-you-render, the React Profiler API for measuring in production, and Web Vitals like Interaction to Next Paint, which measures the exact thing we tuned: input responsiveness.

lecture_title: 6.2 - Where from Here?
text: Finally, a challenge. Pick a real component in a project you work on, one you suspect is slow, and write down its current number from the Profiler before changing anything. Then apply exactly one technique from this course and measure again. Share the before and after with someone, because explaining a measured improvement is the best way to cement it. Thank you for sticking with it, for typing in that laggy filter box more times than any reasonable person should, and for building the habit of measuring first. Go make something fast, on purpose. I'll see you in the next course.
